If you have ever read a book that has a short section at the beginning — before Chapter 1 — where the author says things like "This book is about…" or "Before we begin, I want to explain why I wrote this…" — that section is called a preface. It is not the main content. It is a warm-up. It prepares you for everything that comes after it.

The adjective prefatory simply means: of the nature of a preface — that is, something that introduces, prepares, or sets the stage for the main thing, rather than being the main thing itself.

Think of it this way: if the main event is a concert, the prefatory part is the opening act — it exists to get you ready, not to be the highlight.

"Prefatory" is used to describe words, remarks, sections, or material that come before the real substance of something and serve to introduce it. It answers the question: "What is this, and why are you reading/hearing it?"

Something prefatory typically does one or more of these jobs:

  • Explains the purpose of what follows
  • Provides background context the audience needs
  • Acknowledges something before getting to the point
  • Sets the tone or scope of what's coming
  • Offers a disclaimer or caveat upfront

Here are examples that show the word in natural use:

  • "Before his speech, the professor made a few prefatory remarks about the history of the topic."
    → He said a few things to introduce and frame his main speech, not to deliver the speech itself.
  • "The book opens with a prefatory note from the editor explaining how the manuscript was discovered."
    → That note is not the book's content — it is an introduction to the book's content.
  • "She began her presentation with prefatory comments about why the data was collected."
    → She warmed up the audience with context before diving into the actual data.
  • "Skip the prefatory pages if you already know the author's background."
    → Those pages exist to introduce you to background information, not to deliver the core argument.
The Crucial Distinction: What Prefatory Is Not

This is where many learners get a little fuzzy, so let's be precise.

Something prefatory is not a random digression or an off-topic comment. It is deliberately placed before the main content to serve and support it. It is intentional and functional — like a doorstep that exists specifically to help you enter the house properly.

Also, "prefatory" does not mean unimportant. Prefatory material can be deeply insightful — it just belongs to the introduction layer, not the substance layer. A preface to a novel might be one of the most beautifully written parts of the book, yet it is still prefatory because its role is to prepare, not to be the main story.

"Prefatory" carries a slightly formal tone. You are more likely to encounter it in academic writing, literary criticism, formal speeches, professional reports, or quality journalism than in everyday casual conversation. If a friend says "Before I tell you the story, let me just say…" — those words are prefatory in meaning, but in casual speech, nobody would use the word itself. In a published essay or a courtroom address, however, "These prefatory remarks will be brief" fits naturally.
One Sentence to Lock It In

Prefatory describes anything — a remark, a note, a section, a paragraph — that comes before the main content in order to introduce, contextualize, or prepare the audience for it.

If you can remember that preface = introduction, then prefatory = having the character of an introduction, you will never confuse this word again.
